694.title: Your Nitnem now
694.hook: write down what your daily prayer is now, however small
694.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada sets a daily Nitnem of morning banis, Rehras at dusk and Kirtan Sohila at night; initiated Sikhs keep it as part of their discipline, and many others build toward it at their own pace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long hymns: Sukhmani, Asa di Var, the Barah Maha and the ninth Guru's saloks. Did something get more time than it strictly needed? Today, something shorter, and more personal. Day six hundred ninety-four.

Here's an honest question, the kind a friend asks on a long walk: what do you actually do, most days? Not what you planned in January. Not what an ideal person does. What really happens on an ordinary Wednesday, between waking and sleep? Maybe it's one breath before you reach for your phone. Maybe a shabad on the drive to work. Maybe nothing yet. Every one of those is a real answer. Today, a word Sikhs use for that question, and a pen. Your Nitnem now.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU ACTUALLY DO, MOST DAYS?` → `NOT THE PLAN. THE WEDNESDAY.` → `A WORD, AND A PEN.`

segments.voice: Nitnem means the daily rule. In Punjabi, nit is daily, and nem is a rule or a vow. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada published by the SGPC, sets out a Nitnem for Sikhs: the Japji, the Jaap and the ten Savaiye in the morning, Rehras at dusk, Kirtan Sohila at night. Some Sikhs also say Chaupai and Anand in the morning. That's the full shape, the banis we walked through two days ago. Initiated Sikhs take it on as part of their rehat. Others grow into it slowly: a grandmother who says all of it before dawn, a student who listens to the Japji on the bus, a father who says Sohila beside a child's bed. Sikh teaching gives a reason the rule matters, and it isn't keeping score. In the Japji, Guru Nanak names the amritvela, the ambrosial hours before dawn, as the time to dwell on the true Name and the greatness of God. A rule is a way of keeping that appointment on mornings when the feeling isn't there. And Sikhs say just as plainly that recitation without attention is hollow; the Savaiye you learned this year make that point about ritual without love. So the rule and the heart are meant to travel together. For someone learning about this path, or walking beside a Sikh partner or parent, a daily practice might start very small: a line, a minute, a shabad. Sikhs who keep the full Nitnem would add that the full one is the rehat for the initiated, and a small start is a start, not the whole. The app isn't setting a rule today. It's asking what yours is, right now, honestly.
screen: `NIT AND NEM: DAILY, AND A RULE.` · `THE REHAT'S NITNEM: MORNING, DUSK, NIGHT.` · `AMRITVELA: KEEPING THE APPOINTMENT.` · `THE RULE AND THE HEART, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `MY NITNEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write it. Find paper, or your notes app. At the top, write two words: my nitnem. Underneath, write what you actually do now, however small. One breath and Waheguru. The Japji on Sundays. Rehras playing while you cook. Nothing yet, but I'd like one line in the morning. Keep it true, not impressive. Then put the pen down, read it once, and sit quietly with what you wrote, without grading it. The bell holds the time.
Your Nitnem now. Nitnem, the daily rule: for Sikhs, the set banis of morning, dusk and night; and today, the honest shape of what you do each day.
Your line: my nitnem. Today, do the one thing you wrote down, once, at the time you wrote it for. Day six hundred ninety-four.

695.title: The line you'll keep
695.hook: choose one line from this year to carry into the next
695.howItsDone: Each morning gurdwaras take a hukamnama, opening the Guru Granth Sahib and reading the hymn at the top of the left-hand page, and many Sikhs carry that hymn, or a single line they love, through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your Nitnem now, and your line, my nitnem. Did you do the one thing you wrote down, at the time you wrote it for? Today, from all the words of this year, just one line. Day six hundred ninety-five.

Early each morning at the Darbar Sahib in Amritsar, after the Guru Granth Sahib is carried in and opened, a granthi reads out a single hymn. That one hymn becomes the word for the day. In many gurdwaras it's written on a board near the door. Families send it to each other before breakfast. Someone in London reads the same lines as someone in Ludhiana, and carries them to work. One hymn, held for one day. Today, one line, held for a year. The line you'll keep.
screen: `ONE HYMN, READ AT DAWN.` → `SHARED BEFORE BREAKFAST.` → `ONE LINE, FOR A YEAR.`

segments.voice: That morning hymn is called the hukamnama: the order, or the command, of the day. Hukam is a word from the Japji, the divine order that everything moves within. The hukamnama is that order as a page you can read. The Guru Granth Sahib is opened, not to a favorite place but wherever it opens, and the hymn beginning at the top of the left-hand page is read aloud as the Guru's word for the sangat today. Sikhs do the same at weddings, namings, and the start of new things. Gurdwaras post it, families text it, people turn it over in their heads at red lights. So the habit of holding one piece of bani for a stretch of time is an old Sikh habit. Today asks for something longer: one line, held for a year. Here are a few from this year to choose among. Namastvam akaale: salutation to the One beyond time. Hamree karo hath dai rachhaa: give me Your hand and keep me safe. Anand bhaiaa meree maae: I am in bliss, O my mother. Sukhmani's refrain: the jewel of peace is God's ambrosial Name. The ninth Guru: the wise one frightens no one and fears no one. Or a line from the Ardas: the good of all. Choose the line that asks something of you, not just the one that sounds good. Sikhs often say a line of bani works slowly; you come back to it and it keeps opening. You'll hear it differently in March than in October. One more thing. These are words Sikhs treat as the living Guru, so many write them out carefully and keep them somewhere clean and respectful. Pick a place you'd be glad to look at.
screen: `HUKAMNAMA: THE DAY'S ORDER FROM THE GRANTH.` · `ONE HYMN, CARRIED THROUGH ONE DAY.` · `A HANDFUL OF LINES FROM THIS YEAR.` · `CHOOSE THE LINE THAT ASKS SOMETHING.` · then, large: `ONE LINE, KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose, then write. Close your eyes and let a few lines from this year pass by, slowly, like a scroll. Notice which one your mind stops on. That's probably yours. Open your eyes and write it out, by hand if you can, in English, in Punjabi, or both. Then put it where you'll see it: inside a notebook cover, a card by your bed, the first page of your journal. For the rest of the time, sit and let the line repeat, quietly. The bell holds the time.
The line you'll keep. One line of bani, chosen from this year, written down, and carried into the next, the way a hukamnama is carried through a day.
Your line: one line, kept. Today, read your chosen line three times: when you wake, at midday, and before you sleep. Day six hundred ninety-five.

696.title: Year two close
696.hook: the day now begins and ends in the Guru's words; next year, the long story
696.howItsDone: Many Sikhs begin the day at amritvela with the morning banis and end it with Kirtan Sohila, understanding the bani itself as the Guru whose company they keep through the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the line you'll keep, and your line, one line, kept. Did you read it three times, morning, midday and night? Today is the last day of year two. Day six hundred ninety-six.

Day three hundred thirty-two. The Jaap Sahib, for the first time: fast meters, unfamiliar names, praise rolling past faster than you could follow. Since then you've heard the morning prayers, the dusk prayer, the night song, a psalm of peace in twenty-four parts, a ballad for dawn, twelve months of longing, the ninth Guru's calm, and the Ardas, line by line. Somewhere along the way the strangeness wore into something else. Familiar, maybe. Today: year two close.
screen: `DAY 332: THE JAAP, FOR THE FIRST TIME.` → `A YEAR OF BANIS.` → `STRANGE, THEN FAMILIAR.`

segments.voice: Look at the shape of it. Year one gave you the path's words, its stories, its practices and the Japji. Year two gave you a day. The amritvela and the Japji, the Jaap and the Savaiye. Chaupai and Anand. Rehras when work ends. Sohila when the lights go off. Around that day, longer rhythms: Sukhmani for the hard seasons, Asa di Var before sunrise, the Barah Maha on the first of each month, the ninth Guru's saloks near the Granth's close, and the Ardas, said standing, at the start and end of gatherings and undertakings. Why does this matter so much to Sikhs? Guru Ram Das gives an answer in a hymn on Ang 982: the bani is the Guru, and the Guru is the bani, and within the bani is all the nectar. For Sikhs, if the words are the Guru, then a day spent in the words is a day spent in the Guru's company. That's what the daily banis are, seen from the inside: not a list of tasks, but company, from before dawn to after dark. And it explains the week behind you, too, when the Granth itself was named Guru. Now turn and face the other way. Year three is the long story: Sikh history told slowly, beginning with its first tellers. Tomorrow you meet Bhai Gurdas, who wrote out the Adi Granth in his own hand for Guru Arjan and composed forty vars of his own. After him comes Bhai Nand Lal, a poet who sat with the Tenth Guru. The voices you learned this year become the voices in that story. When the Gurus speak in year three, you'll already know how they sound.
screen: `YEAR TWO: A DAY IN THE GURU'S WORDS.` · `THE LONGER RHYTHMS AROUND THE DAY.` · `THE BANI IS THE GURU.` · `YEAR THREE: THE LONG STORY.` · then, large: `THE DAY, IN HIS WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest, and look ahead. Sit back, let your shoulders drop, and do nothing for a little while. Let the year settle like dust in a quiet room. Then picture tomorrow morning, the moment just after you wake. Picture the line you kept yesterday, or one word, Waheguru, arriving there first, before the to-do list, before the news. If you pray, you can let that word be the first thing you say tomorrow. If you don't, simply let the morning have a little room in it. The bell holds the time.
Year two close. The end of the daily banis: a year in which the day came to begin and end in the Guru's words, with the long story of year three ahead.
Your line: the day, in his words. Tonight, let the last thing you hear before sleep be the Guru's words: your kept line, or a few minutes of Sohila. Day six hundred ninety-six. Year two, done.

697.title: The scribe of the Granth
697.hook: a man writes out the Guru's hymns word for word, and keeps his own poems beside the book
697.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Gurdas as the scribe of the Adi Granth, and his vars are sung and explained in gurdwaras alongside gurbani, though they are not part of the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, year two closed, and your line was the day, in his words. Were the last words you heard last night the Guru's? Year three starts now. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

One man reads a hymn aloud, slowly. Another dips his pen, writes down every word, and waits for the next line. Sikh tradition remembers a scene like that: Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, gathering the hymns of the Gurus before him, and a learned Sikh named Bhai Gurdas writing them out into one great volume, the Adi Granth. Year three is the long story, Sikh history told slowly. And every long story needs someone who writes things down. Today: the scribe of the Granth.
screen: `ONE MAN READS.` → `ANOTHER WRITES EVERY WORD.` → `THE LONG STORY BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Who was he? Tradition remembers Bhai Gurdas as a relative of the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. Tradition also says he grew up close to the Gurus' household, with the hymns around him. When Guru Arjan gathered the Guru's word into one book, tradition says Bhai Gurdas was the one holding the pen while the Guru dictated. It's a strange and humble job. Your hand moves, but the words aren't yours. A scribe who adds a flourish of his own, or fixes a line he'd have written differently, has failed at the one thing a scribe is for. The whole skill is faithfulness. Now the twist. This same man was a poet with a voice of his own. He composed vars, Punjabi ballads, about the Gurus and the Sikh way of life. And he did not slip them into the volume he was writing out. His vars stand beside the Granth, never inside it. He knew exactly which words were the Guru's and which were his, and he never blurred the line. Sikhs still sing his work. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the community's code of conduct, names the writings of Bhai Gurdas among those that may be sung as kirtan in the gurdwara, alongside gurbani, the Guru's own word. So the scribe's voice still sounds in the room, next to the book he copied, and never mistaken for it. And here's why year three begins with him. Bhai Gurdas is also a teller of the Sikh story. His first var tells of Guru Nanak's life and travels. Over the coming days, we'll walk through that var.
screen: `A RELATIVE OF GURU AMAR DAS.` · `THE SCRIBE: FAITHFUL HANDS.` · `THE POET: HIS VARS BESIDE THE GRANTH.` · `A TELLER OF THE STORY.` · then, large: `THE SCRIBE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line by hand, carefully. Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Choose a line you know: the line you kept from last year, a line of the Mool Mantar, or just one word, Waheguru. Write it slowly, letter by letter, as if the page might outlast you. Don't add anything. Don't decorate it. When it's finished, read it back once and check every word against the original. That's the scribe's whole craft: care, and nothing of your own slipped in. If you pray, you can say the line under your breath as you write. The bell holds the time.
The scribe of the Granth. Bhai Gurdas, who, tradition says, wrote out the Adi Granth for Guru Arjan, and whose own vars Sikhs still sing beside it.
screen: `THE SCRIBE OF THE GRANTH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the scribe. Today, when you pass on someone else's words, a message, a recipe, a quote, pass them on exactly, with no spin of your own. Day six hundred ninety-seven.

698.title: The key to the Granth
698.hook: tradition says Guru Arjan called Bhai Gurdas's vars the key to understanding the Guru's word
698.howItsDone: Sikh tradition describes Bhai Gurdas's vars as the key to the Guru Granth Sahib, and speakers in the gurdwara may draw on them when explaining a hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scribe of the Granth, and your line, the scribe. Did you pass someone's words on exactly, with nothing added? Day six hundred ninety-eight.

What's the smallest object in your home that does the most work? There's a good case for the key. A strip of metal that fits in your palm, and without it, the whole house stays shut. You can stand on the step with the lights on inside and still not get in. Sikh tradition reaches for exactly that object when it talks about Bhai Gurdas, the scribe we met yesterday. Today's word: kunji. The key.
screen: `THE SMALLEST THING THAT DOES THE MOST.` → `A HOUSE STAYS SHUT WITHOUT IT.` → `KUNJI.`

segments.voice: Kunji is the Punjabi word for a key. Tradition says Guru Arjan spoke of Bhai Gurdas's vars as the key to the Guru's word: the kunji of the Granth. It's a saying handed down by the community, not a line written in the Granth itself, so it's held as tradition. But it has stuck, and it's worth turning over. First, a key is not the house. Nobody lives in a key. You don't hang pictures on it or cook in it. Its whole job is to get you through a door and then go back in your pocket. That's the place Sikhs give the vars: not beside the Guru's word as an equal, and never in place of it, but at the door, helping someone in. Second, a key is shaped by the lock. Its teeth only make sense because of the door they fit. Bhai Gurdas's vars keep returning to ideas the Gurus sing in the Granth: the gurmukh, the Guru's faithful follower, and the sangat, the holy company. He takes those ideas and unfolds them in plain pictures and stories, in Punjabi, so a listener can find a way in. Third, a key gets used, not admired. In katha, the spoken explanation of a hymn in the gurdwara, a speaker may reach for a line of Bhai Gurdas the way you reach for a key at the front door, without fuss, to open something bigger. That's the order the saying sets: the vars serve the hymn. They open a door, and step aside.
screen: `KUNJI: THE KEY.` · `A KEY IS NOT THE HOUSE.` · `SHAPED BY THE LOCK IT OPENS.` · `USED, NOT ADMIRED.` · then, large: `THE KEY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find a key in your house. Any key: the front door, a bike lock, a drawer. Hold it in your open hand. Feel its weight, run a thumb along its teeth. Then let it bring someone to mind: a person who opened something for you. A teacher who made a hard subject make sense. A grandparent who explained a prayer. A friend who showed you the way into a place you'd been standing outside of. Stay with that person for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. The bell holds the time.
Kunji. A key: the name tradition gives to Bhai Gurdas's vars, which open the door to the Guru's word and then step aside.
Your line: the key. Today, when you help someone understand something, open the door and then step aside. Let them walk in on their own. Day six hundred ninety-eight.

699.title: The world before Nanak
699.hook: his first var describes a dark age of empty ritual and quarrels over labels, before Nanak came
699.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Bhai Gurdas's first var hear its opening stanzas as the backdrop to Guru Nanak's coming: a world where outward signs and rivalries had crowded out devotion to the one Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kunji, and your line, the key. Did you open a door for someone and then step aside? Today we use the key for the first time. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

Truth, left standing on the bank, while two men quarrel themselves to ruin. That's one of the pictures Bhai Gurdas paints in his first var, before Guru Nanak has even been born into the story. Before the hero walks on, a storyteller shows what's wrong with the world he walks into. Bhai Gurdas spends a good stretch of his first var doing exactly that, and he doesn't go easy. Today: the world before Nanak.
screen: `TRUTH, LEFT ON THE BANK.` → `SETTING THE STAGE.` → `THE WORLD BEFORE NANAK.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas calls it the kalyug, the dark age. And look at what he says is dark. Not a lack of religion. There's plenty of religion in his picture. People divided into castes on one side and into rival schools on the other. Hindus heading for the Ganges and Banaras, Muslims for Mecca and the Kaaba. One side proud of the sacred thread and the forehead mark, the other of its own outward signs. Both call on God, Ram for some, Rahim for others, and Bhai Gurdas says it's one Name, but they lose their way on two roads. Pride, stubbornness and quarreling fill the space where devotion should be. And then the line from the hook: truth stood off on the bank while the Brahmin and the maulvi wore each other out. Hear this carefully, because it's easy to mishear. Bhai Gurdas isn't attacking Hindus, or Muslims, or their scriptures. In the same passage he says people forgot what their own books taught. His target is what happens when a label, a mark or a place of pilgrimage becomes the whole of faith, and the people under the labels stop seeing each other. He is painting a mood in the world, not grading anyone's religion. That's the darkness: ritual with nobody home, and neighbors turned rivals over names for the same God. Then, at the end of the stretch, the turn. Bhai Gurdas says the generous Lord heard the cry of the world, and sent Guru Nanak into it. The stage is set. The light comes tomorrow.
screen: `THE KALYUG: A DARK AGE.` · `PLENTY OF RELIGION, LITTLE TRUTH.` · `ONE NAME, TWO ROADS, ONE QUARREL.` · `THE CRY IS HEARD.` · then, large: `BEFORE THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one empty ritual in your own life. Not a religious one, necessarily. A habit you go through with nobody home. Saying "fine" when someone asks how you are. Scrolling the same three apps before you get out of bed. A thank you you say without looking up. Find just one. Don't scold yourself for it. Just sit with it for the length of the bell and ask what it was once meant to be for. If you pray, you can ask for that one thing to be filled again. The bell holds the time.
The world before Nanak. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, a dark age of labels, quarrels and empty ritual, with truth left standing on the bank, until the cry was heard.
Your line: before the light. Today, take the one empty ritual you found and do it once with someone home: say how you really are, or look up for the thank you. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

700.title: The mist cleared
700.hook: the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared and light spread through the world (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1.27)
700.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, this stanza of Bhai Gurdas's first var may be sung as kirtan or explained in katha, as a picture of Guru Nanak's coming.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world before Nanak, and your line, before the light. Did you fill one empty ritual with something real? Day seven hundred.

A winter morning on a country road. Fog so thick the headlights reach the next post and stop. Everything is gray: the fields, the trees, the road itself. You drive slowly, guessing. And then, without anyone deciding it, the sun gets high enough. The fog thins, lifts, and is simply gone, and the whole road is there, the fields on either side, a farmhouse you didn't know was close. Nothing new was added. It was all there already. Today: the mist cleared.
screen: `FOG ON A WINTER ROAD.` → `THE SUN GETS HIGH ENOUGH.` → `IT WAS ALL THERE ALREADY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhai Gurdas set the stage: a dark age, truth standing off on the bank. Today, a few stanzas on in his first var, the light arrives, and he reaches for big pictures. The true Guru Nanak appeared, he says. The mist cleared, and there was light in the world. It was like the sun coming up: the stars hide and the darkness runs off. And like a lion's roar, at which the herd of deer scatters and can't hold its ground. Notice what kind of picture this is. Bhai Gurdas doesn't say Nanak built a new world. He says the mist cleared. A sunrise doesn't create the road, the fields or the farmhouse. It shows what was already standing there. In Sikh teaching, the One was never absent from the world. What had gone missing was the seeing. Then Bhai Gurdas goes on to say what that light looked like on the ground, and it's surprisingly homely. Wherever Baba set his foot, a place of worship grew up. In house after house there was a dharamsal, a place for the sangat to gather, and kirtan sung, and it felt like a festival every day. That's how Bhai Gurdas measures the light: not in thunder, but in ordinary homes where people started to gather, sit together and sing. And it fits what you learned in year two. The daily banis are exactly that kind of light. Small. Repeated. Kept in houses. A dawn that comes again tomorrow.
screen: `THE SUN RISES, THE STARS HIDE.` · `NOT A NEW WORLD: THE MIST CLEARED.` · `A DHARAMSAL IN HOUSE AFTER HOUSE.` · `LIGHT, KEPT IN ORDINARY HOMES.` · then, large: `THE MIST CLEARED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a curtain. If there's a window near you, go and open the blind or the curtain all the way, even if it's already light, even if it's night and there's only a streetlamp. Then sit facing it. Let your eyes rest on what was already there: a wall, a tree, a rooftop, the sky. Nothing new has been added to the room. You've only let it be seen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly as the light comes in. The bell holds the time.
The mist cleared. Bhai Gurdas's picture of Guru Nanak's coming: not a new world made, but the fog lifting from the one that was already there.
Your line: the mist cleared. Today, look again at one person or place you've stopped seeing. Let the fog lift off it for a minute. Day seven hundred.
